questions.stem: A man is diagnosed with a condition that significantly raises the temperature inside the scrotum. What is the most likely effect on his fertility?

options.text: Increased sperm production because higher temperatures speed up cell division
No effect, because sperm production is not affected by temperature
Reduced sperm production because sperm develop best at temperatures slightly below body temperature
Increased testosterone production leading to more sperm

questions.explanation: The testes are located outside the body in the scrotum because sperm production (spermatogenesis) requires a temperature about 2 degrees C below core body temperature. If scrotal temperature rises significantly, sperm production is impaired, reducing fertility.

questions.stem: A student examines a diagram showing the male reproductive system. Which pathway correctly describes the route sperm travel from production to leaving the body?

options.text: Testes -> urethra -> sperm duct -> penis
Testes -> sperm duct -> urethra -> penis
Epididymis -> testes -> sperm duct -> penis
Sperm duct -> testes -> urethra -> penis

questions.explanation: Sperm are produced in the testes, mature in the epididymis, then travel through the sperm duct (vas deferens) where they mix with seminal fluid from the seminal vesicles and prostate gland. They then pass through the urethra and out via the penis during ejaculation.

questions.stem: Seminal fluid contains fructose sugar and is alkaline. How do these properties help sperm reach and fertilise the egg?

options.text: Fructose kills bacteria, and the alkaline pH speeds up sperm swimming
Fructose provides energy for sperm movement, and the alkaline pH neutralises the acidic conditions in the vagina
Fructose makes the sperm sticky so they attach to the egg, and alkaline pH dissolves the egg membrane
Fructose increases the number of sperm produced, and alkaline pH prevents the sperm from drying out

questions.explanation: Fructose in seminal fluid is an energy source that fuels the movement of sperm tails as they swim towards the egg. The alkaline nature of seminal fluid neutralises the acidic environment of the vagina, which would otherwise kill sperm. Both adaptations increase the chance of successful fertilisation.

questions.stem: A patient undergoes a vasectomy, in which the sperm ducts are cut and tied. What is the effect of this procedure?

options.text: Sperm are still released during ejaculation but cannot swim
Testosterone production stops, reducing male characteristics
Sperm cannot reach the urethra, so ejaculate contains no sperm
The testes stop producing sperm entirely

questions.explanation: A vasectomy cuts the sperm ducts (vas deferens), preventing sperm from travelling from the testes to the urethra. The testes still produce sperm and testosterone, so male characteristics are unaffected. Ejaculation still occurs but the fluid contains no sperm, making conception impossible.

questions.stem: Millions of sperm are released during ejaculation, yet only one fertilises the egg. Which statement best explains why so many sperm are needed?

options.text: Most sperm are genetically defective and cannot survive
Multiple sperm are needed to penetrate the egg membrane simultaneously
Many sperm die in the acidic vaginal environment or fail to reach the egg, so large numbers increase the chance of one reaching the egg
The extra sperm provide nutrients for the egg after fertilisation

questions.explanation: The journey from the vagina to the oviduct is hostile: the acidic pH kills many sperm, and the distance is enormous relative to sperm size. Many sperm swim in the wrong direction or become trapped. Releasing millions maximises the probability that at least one healthy sperm will reach and fertilise the egg.
